title: Quoting Jack Despain Zhou
content:
Among the many already existing effects of AI has been a great de-individualization. I open a YouTube video, and I hear Claude. I sit in a conference presentation, and I hear Claude. I open my email inbox, and I find pitches and articles from ostensibly serious people with ostensibly serious credentials attached to ostensibly serious institutions who want to publish things attached to their reputations and mine, and I see Claude.

— Jack Despain Zhou, Spitting in the Face of Glaude

title: ★ Obvious Affordances Are Due for a Comeback
content:
Speaking of Marcin Wichary, like me, he’s a big user of Apple Notes. Unlike me, he’s such a big user of Notes that he (somehow) uses Notes as the CMS for the whole Unsung blog. In a post this week, he wrote about how Notes — like file systems and most other notes apps — keeps two dates for each note: created and modified. You can sort your list of notes in Notes by either date; the default is by modification date, which Notes calls “edited”. Conveniently, Notes will remember your sorting preference on a per-folder basis. So if you have a folder of notes that you use as a journal, you can sort that folder by date created, without affecting the sort order for your other folders. (Notes only remembers each folder’s sort-by order per device, so if you use multiple devices, you’ll need to change the sort-by setting for a given folder on each device.)

In the editing view for a single note, however, Notes only shows one date, the modified/edited date, like so:

November 26, 2026 at 1:00 pm

Wichary writes:

This can feel frustrating. You know the data is there, you see it in the left pane, part of the software recognizes and supports it, but there seems to be no way to summon it in a place you want. I looked through the context (right click) menus, and through the main menu. I couldn’t find anything, and I assumed that possibility just wasn’t there.

Then recently, years on, I accidentally clicked on the timestamp, and this happened:

[Screen capture movie omitted.]

That click was what I needed all along. Clicking alternates between “created” and “edited” timestamps. It even puts a little prefix not just before the other date, but before both.

Yet… there is really no way to know this functionality is there.

Clicking the timestamp to toggle between the edited and created dates is a cool hidden feature. But as Wichary notes, why is it hidden?

I don’t necessarily mean that Notes had to do something like what Finder or Bear do, and expose that data all the time — that kind of stuff can feel heavy. But I think it’s important to make sure all actions have their entry points somewhere where you can discover them. Maybe it’s the main menu, maybe it’s the right-click menu. I’m a fan of command palettes in part because that’s where more esoteric options can go without overloading other surfaces.

On the Mac, there probably ought to be an item in the View menu for this. But that wouldn’t help on iOS, which has no menu bar. The basic problem is that the timestamp at the top of every note is clickable, but it doesn’t look clickable. If clicking on something does something, that thing should look clickable. Just what “looking clickable” means is open for debate, but ought to be part of the standard visual language for the platform. It could look like a raised button. It could look like a recessed well. You could keep it flat and just draw a faint button shape behind the text. You could design something exuberantly fun, like making it look and animate like a train station split-flap display. You could be lazy and just underline the text — underlining, although gross, would at least be something. Things that are inert should look inert; things that are clickable should look clickable.1

This gets to the heart of the problem with Apple’s too-minimal UI language — and the rest of the industry mindlessly following Apple’s lead. There’s a wonderful rule of thumb oft attributed to Albert Einstein: Everything should be made as simple as possible, but not simpler.

When clickable UI elements do not look clickable, they’ve been made too simple.

One More Thing

I long ago noticed, somehow, that the timestamps atop notes in Notes2 are clickable, to toggle between edited and created dates. But Wichary’s post brought to my attention a detail that I consider a violation of good design. When you first display a note, the timestamp at the top looks like this:

November 26, 2026 at 1:00 pm

That’s the edited date (which I really want to call “modified”) — but it doesn’t say so. It just shows the date. When you click it, it changes to:

Created: October 31, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Click again and you get:

Edited: November 26, 2026 at 1:00 pm

If you continue clicking, it keeps toggling between the timestamps with the “Created:” and “Edited:” prefix labels. The design violation I’m flagging is that the initial state doesn’t have a label, and there’s no way to get back to the initial unlabeled timestamp. If repeatedly clicking something cycles through multiple states, you should wind up exactly where you started. With these timestamps in Notes, the only way to get back to where you started — a timestamp with no label — is to close the note and reopen it. That’s clearly wrong.

This is a foul, not a bug. It’s a deliberate design decision. And I think we can presume how Apple arrived at this design. The solution I’d like to see is for the date to always be labeled — “Edited:” or “Created:”. Then clicking would just toggle between the two states. With two clicks, you’d be right back where you started. I think always showing these labels would also offer a gentle hint that you can click to change which date is shown. That’s not enough to fully suggest clickability, but it’d be better than nothing, which is what we have now. I’m guessing that the “simpler than possible” minimalist cohort at Apple complained that showing the “Edited:” label from the start is ugly clutter. So, we wound up with this unsatisfying compromise: no label at the start, but toggling between “Created:” and “Edited:” after you click on the timestamp.

Needless clutter ought to be omitted. Some elements are reasonably made optional. But when an item in an app has two timestamps associated with it, labeling which date is which isn’t clutter. Clarity is good. Eliminating ambiguity is good. Liking the way something looks should never come at the expense of conveying an understanding of how it works, or making it harder to use. If you’re not excited by the challenge of designing a presentation for the Notes timestamp that both looks good and suggests that it’s a clickable toggle, you are not a UI designer. You’re a graphic designer.

Dan Wineman wrote a good post on visual affordances back in 2013, just days after Apple unveiled iOS 7’s great flattening, which I’ll quote from again:

That’s what affordances do. They operate on the boundary between sight and touch. You see a thing, often from a distance, and its affordances give you enough information to simulate, in your mind, the sensation of manipulating it. Unconsciously, you configure your fine motor system in advance, so that by the time you get to the door handle, your hand is already forming the right shape to grasp it and pull the door open. [...]

Affordances are the baby to skeuomorphism’s bathwater. When they engage our instincts just right, they create an emotional bond, and the unfamiliar becomes inviting. Without them, it’s just pictures under glass. It makes no difference how flat, how deep, how minimal, or how ornate the look-and-feel is if it can’t show us, when we look, how to feel.

This is the way back to the future. We don’t need to invent these designs. We just need to embrace again what we already know.

  1. And things that could be clickable, but are disabled because of the current state of one or more conditions, should look clickable-but-disabled. Temporarily disabled is different from permanently inert, and that difference can and should be conveyed visually. ↩︎︎

  2. I also noticed, long ago, that when the app is named Notes it’s often awkward to talk about notes in the app. Same for Reminders’ reminders, Files’ files, and, most ungainly of all, Shortcuts’ shortcuts. It’s like Abbott and Costello’s “Who’s on First” bit but less funny. What do you use for notes? Notes. That’s what I’m asking, where do you write them? Notes. Do you even keep notes? Absolutely. Where? Notes. Not what, where? Notes. I’ll kill you.

    That said, my original idea for the name of what became Vesper was “What”, with slogans like, “You use What for your notes? Yes.” I still have the domain whatapp.net (which points nowhere). I had the idea before WhatsApp existed; by the time we started working on Vesper at the end of 2012, though, WhatsApp did exist, so the name What was out the door. That was probably for the best. ↩︎

Charles Koch is a cult leader (permalink)

I've never met Charles Koch, but I sometimes feel like I know him, because he's such a type, instantly recognizable from his philosophy, actions, and pronouncements.

Koch is clearly very smart, in the specific sense of sometimes being able to spot and act on true things that other people either can't see or can't bring themselves to pursue. When he inherited his father's fossil fuel empire, he made a series of investments in innovative processes that would substantially improve the efficiency of the operations, but would also take a very long time to pay off.

These kinds of long-term capital investments are seriously out of fashion in big business, to the extent that the telecom giant Frontier walked away from a billion dollar ROI on fiber rollouts, because the payoff was a decade in the future, and influential market analysts were hostile to any company that made investments that took more than five years to pay off.

Frontier executives' compensation was primarily stock-based, which means that those analysts could instantly make any executive who behaved in ways they disapproved of significantly poorer. So instead of pursuing long-term, substantial growth, Frontier chose short-term enshittification, for example by raising prices and cutting maintenance for over 1m customers who had no other ISPs to choose from. As a result, the company was forced to declare bankruptcy:

https://pluralistic.net/2020/05/01/icann-can-and-did/#fiber-now

This kind of story is why Koch is so openly hostile to the public markets, heaping scorn on founders who take their companies public. Koch was empirically right about how to run his father's business: a decade after he made those long-term investments the public markets wouldn't have tolerated, Koch Industries' profits had increased by 1,000%.

Koch credits his extreme wealth and power to his superior intellect and temperament, boasting of his capacity for delayed gratification. This worship of patience and long-term consideration is a common theme among business leaders and people who venerate them as our civilization's natural and deserving autocrats.

The veneration of a long-term outlook is at the heart of market fundamentalists' self-mythologizing as the keepers of "reason" and "rationalism." Anyone who sits below them on the social and economic hierarchy must be in thrall to their emotions, while those at the top of the system must have conquered their feelings (which facts famously don't care about!) so now they can see the world as it truly is.

There's a whole body of pseudoscience, junk science, and debunked science they promote in support of this proposition. For example, these people love the "marshmallow test," in which children were left alone with a marshmallow and the promise of two marshmallows if they abstained from eating it. Long-term followups found a significant correlation between the children who abstained and long-term economic and professional success.

But the marshmallow test is bunk. The kids who ate the marshmallow were overwhelmingly from poor and marginalized backgrounds and had long experience of adults promising them rewards that never materialized. They'd come to the entirely rational conclusion that if there's a chance to get a treat now, you should take it, rather than waiting for inconstant and unreliable authority figures to make good on their promises of jam tomorrow.

Because those kids were poor and marginalized, they were more likely to face systemic discrimination and barriers in life, barriers that the wealthier, more privileged kids who held out for two marshmallows rarely encountered. Those wealthier kids were born on third base, so they scored more runs than the one-marshmallow kids who rarely got called out of the dugout.

Far from proving that reason, self-denial and self-control are correlated with success, the experiment proved that rich people pass on their privilege to their offspring, who have an easier time in life no matter how defective their judgment and how error-prone their actions.

Which is not to claim that there's no value in a long-term outlook. Charles Koch's long-range planning made Koch Industries far more profitable than its short-termist competitors. But Charles Koch is hardly a paragon of reason: perhaps more than anyone else in the world, he embodies Upton Sinclair's maxim that "It is difficult to get a man to understand something when his salary depends on his not understanding it."

That's because Charles Koch, for all of his self-aggrandized long-termism, is one of the world's most ardent and important climate change deniers. Koch's intellectual contributions to climate denial are significant, but they're nothing compared to his financial contributions. There is no climate crackpot so unhinged, no junk science so flimsy, no conspiracy so absurd that Koch will not respond with showers of cash, buying their way into our discourse.

This is motivated reasoning. After all, Koch owes his fortune, his power and his influence to burning fossil fuels. Moreover, he attributes that power and privilege to the market's infallible ability to elevate the wise and worthy. That's how he claims to be a champion of "personal liberty," despite his ability to decide how so many millions of the rest of us must live our lives.

For Koch, the purpose of "liberty" is to allow each of us to audition in front of the market's self-regulating selection mechanism, so that the best among us (coolly rational and long-term in outlook) can be put in charge of the rest, in order to save them from their flawed emotionality and impulsivity.

For Koch to acknowledge the obvious and worsening climate emergency would require him to shutter his coal plants: no one who believes in climate science could claim a "long-term" outlook while pumping gigatons of CO2 into the atmosphere. But even worse: acknowledging climate science means repudiating market orthodoxy.

There is no greater indictment of the idea that allowing markets to self-regulate will lead to our collective prosperity than the climate emergency and the existential threat it represents to human civilization. Likewise, there is no greater indictment of markets' ability to select the wisest among us to rule over us than the fact that the market's chosen champions have committed themselves to driving our civilization, our species and the habitability of our planet over a cliff.

Koch is a long-termist, but only when a long-term view serves his personal prejudices and privilege. The rest of the time, Koch breaks all speed records when he gobbles down that marshmallow. And because "the market" has given Koch so much power, he's eating all our marshmallows:

https://locusmag.com/feature/cory-doctorow-marshmallow-longtermism/

Koch is no rationalist. There is nothing more irrational than committing your fortune to destroying the civilization that it depends on. No one can lay claim to cool reason while they are busily sawing through the branch they're sitting on.

I'm not claiming that any of the rest of us are any better. We are, all of us, inconstant in our rationality; we are all capable of self-deception and motivated reasoning. But most of us know it. We may not like being in a situation where other people can call us on our bullshit, but in our hearts of hearts, we know that we're better off for it:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/10/09/impunitism/#rats-eating-my-face

Koch is an engineer who exalts reason, but he can't distinguish between his beliefs and "science." When actual scientists perform careful experiments and analysis demonstrating that Koch needs to shut down his coal empire, his answers are, "Well that's your opinion" and "if you're so smart, why aren't you rich?"

This inability to distinguish between your cherished delusions and objective reality is the most dangerous of all forms of emotion-driven self-sabotage. No one is more prone to this folly than the ultra-rich who have insulated themselves from consequences or even disagreement:

https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/09/autocrats-of-trade-2/#witness-the-firepower-of-this-fully-armed-and-operational-battle-station

Koch declares whatever he believes in to be "science." Take Koch's management philosophy, "Market Process Analysis," which he has declared to be a "science of liberty." Workers in Koch's empires are required to devote hours every week to studying this "science" and its precepts, despite the fact that his firms routinely ignore many of those tenets (such as "respect," the "ninth guiding principle" of Market Process Analysis).

Writing for Jacobin, the labor historian Henry Snow breaks down the four unproven, self-serving ideological follies that make up this "science":

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economics-workplace-tyranny-markets

First: that "society" does not exist, and can only be understood as a collection of individuals. This "methodological individualism" is extremely convenient for the wealthy and powerful because their fortunes allow them to unilaterally wield enormous power over lots of other people.

Meanwhile, the rest of us can only resist the demands that the rich make of us by wielding collective power, through unions, movements and democratic institutions. Koch's embrace of Thatcher's cheap quip about there being "no such thing as society" is great news for Koch, in other words, and (like so many of Thatcher's maxims) it is a demand dressed up as a truth.

When Koch says "there is no such thing as society, only individuals," he means "you must not ever successfully resist my control by banding together – you must confine your resistance to acting as individuals, because that way you are doomed to fail."

Koch's second principle is that individuals are only motivated by their self-interest ("psychological egoism"). This is likewise very convenient for someone whose power can only endure for so long as the rest of us can't work together to depose them. If Koch can convince you that your comrades and friends are actually only using you to better their own lot, then he can prevent you from making any kind of solidaristic sacrifice to help them (which guarantees that they'll never do the same for you).

The third principle is a form of market fundamentalism: the belief that at a societal level, plans can't ever work, that the only way to steer society is through "self-correcting" markets. Here's another self-serving, convenient rationalization: if the market leaves Koch rich and you poor; if it leaves him comfortable and you struggling; that's just how it is.

If you were to band together to create democratic institutions that tried to build a fairer, better society, you would be doomed to fail, because your planning system could never "incorporate as much information" as the market, which is the world's greatest computer and integrator of "signals" that lead to the most efficient allocation and production possible.

The fourth principle is more market fundamentalism: the belief that "everything is – and should be – a market." In a world of individuals who can only behave selfishly, where all grand plans are doomed to fail, the only way to improve the world and our lot in it is to "create incentives" and "design mechanisms" that let the market make its magic.

As Snow writes, people who espouse these beliefs follow Koch's lead in describing them as "scientific truths," while downgrading every disagreement to mere "ideology." They claim to be moved by facts, while their fuzzy-headed opponents are moved by feelings.

These people are part of a long lineage of "scientific managers" who have come up with doctrines and methods that are sold as ways to improve production and make us all better off, but always turn out to be ways for bosses to atomize, demoralize and control their workers:

https://pluralistic.net/2021/02/24/gwb-rumsfeld-monsters/#bossware

Inevitably, these "scientists" claim to have discovered a freestanding and objective "human nature." But scholars who subject the idea of "human nature" to scientific and historical scrutiny have repeatedly and reliably discovered a wide spectrum of human natures, which are not fixed from birth, but are rather determined by a mix of temperament, societal norms and material reality:

https://pluralistic.net/2022/03/08/three-freedoms/#anti-fatalism

Koch isn't describing the world as it is, he's describing the world as he wishes it was, because that way his wealth and power would be both justified and eternal. Like I say, this is an extremely recognizable type of guy, the kind of person who insists that their preferences are scientific truths.

It's a powerful move, which is why it's the basis of so many cults. Scientology founder L Ron Hubbard's daffy stfnal nonsense owes its decades of success to both its high-pressure control tactics and Hubbard's claims to having discovered an immortal science to sweep aside superstition and folly. But as bonkers as Scientology is, it's no less "scientific" than Market Process Analysis, Charles Koch's "science of liberty."

Market Process Analysis is delivered in the manner of cult doctrine, with Koch's employees forced to spend hours every week studying it. When they are discreetly polled on their experience with the doctrine, they sound like any unhappy cult member, describing it as "brainwashing" and comparing their workplaces to "Nineteen Eighty-Four." They describe how managers exercise unilateral and total authority over their working lives: "managers are GOD…they can play with anyone's life."

Also very Scientology-like are the unsuccessful attempts of workers to better their situations by citing the tenets of Market Process Analysis in a bid to get their managers to treat them better. These workers quickly discover that the cult's doctrine is something they are expected to live by, but not hold their bosses to.

Koch himself insists that Market Process Analysis isn't just a way to organize a workplace, but rather, it is the key to how we should relate to our friends and family. Koch was essentially abandoned by his (Nazi sympathizing) parents, who turned him over to a (Nazi-sympathizing) nanny who required him to shit on command (literally), until she left the family's employ to live in Vichy France and help advance the fascist project there:

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2016/jan/17/dark-money-review-nazi-oil-the-koch-brothers-and-a-rightwing-revolution

This terrible and abusive childhood didn't instill any sense of the importance of love and tolerance in Koch. Far from it: he and his brothers David and William conspired to excommunicate and isolate their oldest brother Frederick as punishment for his open homosexuality:

https://web.archive.org/web/20150208024948/https://www.vanityfair.com/style/society/2014/05/frederick-koch-brothers

My claim here isn't that Koch's flaws are less explainable or more wrong than yours or mine; rather, it's that Koch's inability to acknowledge the possibility that he might be wrong has turned him into an existential threat to the human race and a brutal cult leader. If he wasn't so powerful, he would be hilarious, a self-described "lover of freedom" whose "science of liberty" has to be shoved down the throats of his captive workforce.

title: OGP Image Format Support on Major Sites and Apps
content:
I've built a quick tool to see which image formats are supported on sites that allow Open Graph Protocol link previews.

As I've whinged about before, Facebook have all-but abandoned their efforts to standardise OGP. Which leads to a situation where a bunch of sites all have conflicting requirements on what they'll show. There's no easy way to find out which sites support which image formats, so I've done this manually.

I built OGP Format Tester to see whether social networking sites and apps supported modern formats like AVIF and JPEG-XL. Here are the results of my tests:

AVIF GIF0 JPEG JXL PNG SVG WEBP
Mastodon ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
BlueSky ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Threads ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Facebook ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ✅ ✅
WhatsApp ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
LinkedIn ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Signal ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Telegram ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Slack ❌ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Discord ✅ ❌ 1 ❌2 ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Lemmy ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅3 ✅ ✅ ✅
Teams ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅ ❌ ✅
Discourse ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ✅ ❌ ✅

There's a never ending parade of image formats - but these seven are the ones which seem best supported in all major browsers.

Similarly, I'm sorry if I haven't included your favourite site on here - feel free to leave the results in a comment.

Methodology

I created a simple page like this:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en-GB">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8">
        <title>An OGP Image Test Site for WebP</title>
        <meta property="og:type"         content="website">
        <meta property="og:locale"       content="en_GB">
        <meta property="og:site_name"    content="OGP Site Name">
        <meta property="og:title"        content="OGP Title"> 
        <meta property="og:description"  content="Testing whether WEBP images are displayed in OGP">
        <meta property="og:image"        content="https://ogp.viii.fi/webp.webp">
        <meta property="og:image:type"   content="image/webp">
        <meta property="og:image:width"  content="800">
        <meta property="og:image:height" content="600">
        <meta property="og:image:alt"    content="A WebP Image">
    </head>

That should contain all the metadata necessary for a site to display some preview text and an image.

I then pasted in a URl for each image format into each site. If a preview image came up, they got a tick. If not, a cross.

It's weird that Meta owned Facebook, WhatsApp, and Threads all have slightly different support, and I have no idea why Discord won't show (my?) JPEG previews.

Annoyingly, Facebook, Threads, and Discord are the only ones who support AVIF. JPEG-XL is still a distant dream for most.

Perhaps one day the promise of Web 2.0 will be fully realised and sites will be interoperable with each other.

Testing

If you want to test these yourself, you can use the following URls:

https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=AVIF
https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=GIF
https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=JPEG
https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=JXL
https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=PNG
https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=SVG
https://ogp.viii.fi/ogp.php?format=WEBP

  1. Animated GIF support was only seen on Slack, Threads, Lemmy, Teams, Discourse. The others only displayed the first frame. ↩︎

  2. I suspect Discord want you to post GIFs directly? ↩︎

  3. I tried in several Discord channels, but couldn't get my JPEG to display. ↩︎

  4. Lemmy doesn't proxy images for OGP - it just links directly back to the origin. I'm not sure how secure or sensible that is. ↩︎

title: Underrated reasons to be thankful VI
content:
1. That in most of the world today, you can walk around freely during the day, even in crowds of thousands of people, with almost zero concern that someone will stab you and take your stuff.

  2. That if you’re feeling nauseated, you can apparently pour some isopropyl alcohol onto a pad and sniff it, and the effect is apparently as strong as prescription antiemetics but faster, and this is apparently often used in emergency rooms, although we don’t have great RCTs and no one seems to have the foggiest idea of why it should work and for some reason this trick has utterly failed to entrench itself as a folk remedy.

  3. That your upper body has a vastly higher density of apocrine and sebaceous glands than your legs, so provided you cover your gland-rich groin with underwear, you can skip washing your pants and skirts for a shockingly long time, which is good because work is bad, though even if they (the pants/skirts) still look/smell clean you may still want to wash them occasionally because that will prevent microscopic grime from chewing up the fibers and re-align the weave and (with plant-based fabrics) restore fiber elasticity, thankfully.

  4. That intestinal villi.

  5. That the Earth is struck by lightning a million times a day, creating small fires, and that microbes eat dead stuff, and that if oxygen levels creep up, then you get more small fires which very slowly bring oxygen levels back down, meaning there isn’t enough fuel and oxygen for a single firestorm to grow and self-sustain and consume the planet.

  6. That boring standard best practices, that for 90% of problems, if you just find the boring standard best practices and make a reasonable effort to follow them, you’ll do better than 90% of people, because 90% of people don’t do that, because they’re so boring, which is bad, but you can.

  7. That your great-great-great-great-great-great-great-great-great-grandma breathed air with 280 ppm of CO₂ and all your grandmas before that got 200 to 280 ppm, going back to before those grandmas were human, while if you go outside today you’ll get 432 ppm (ever-increasing), a situation evolution had no reason to prepare for, and given that stuffy air is bad for thinking you might worry what the extra CO₂ is doing to us, but when tested carefully it’s unclear if CO₂ itself has any effect on cognitive performance even at levels ten times higher, so the impact of that extra 152 ppm is probably essentially zero.

  8. That in a modern car, your risk of dying per kilometer is only ⅓ of a similar car from the early 1990s.

  9. That, to keep your eyes working, your body is constantly flushing them with tears, and instead of letting the dirty tears run down your face, your head has an internal tube that drains into the back of your nose where you swallow the tears along with all the dust and bacteria that lands in your eyes—so cool!—and also that this is why liquid comes of your nose when you cry a lot, you are literally crying out of your nose, and also that there’s a valve at the bottom of the tube to prevent snot from going up, thankfully, but if you’re working with a sufficiently large amount of snot it can and sometimes does go up the tube and out your eyes, yes snot can literally come out of your eyes, this is exciting, we like this.

  10. That if you categorize animals by their width/length and height/length ratios, so a shark is longer than it is high or wide, and a sea urchin is equally long and high and wide, then humans are arguably the weirdest:

      W<L W≈L W>L
    H<L snake, worm, shark, crocodile, cat, wolf, ferret, whale, swimming penguin stingray, seaturtle butterfly ray?, gliding albatross?
    H≈L horse, deer, elephant, camel, poodle, angelfish sea urchin, inflated pufferfish? ??
    H>L flamingo, seahorse, giraffe? sea anemone, standing penguin us

  11. That the needs of a human, in sorted order, are: air, safety, heat, water, sleep, food, toilet, medicine, movement, stability, intimacy, community, respect, autonomy, stimulation, privacy, play, purpose, and that most people reading this have to go at halfway through that list before seeing major issues.

  12. That purpose, stupid stubborn purpose, possibly intractable, but if you’re worried about cosmic purpose and you’ve got issues earlier on the list, try fixing them and I bet you won’t feel as worried about cosmic purpose, it’s the nature of the animal.

  13. That music, not something that first principles would suggest should exist.

  14. That in women, urinary continence is achieved by a roughly equal contribution of an internal sphincter, passive tissue, and a pelvic floor + external sphincter, but men after the internal sphincter have a prostate, which creates so much passive resistance that the external sphincter is rarely needed, but sometimes said prostate develops mutations and must be removed along with the internal sphincter, which drops the entire continence workload on a pelvic floor + external sphincter that has been relaxing for 5+ decades, causing leaks, but within a year the pelvic floor + external sphincter typically rise to the occasion, stopping the leaks, and that by doing exercises before and/or after surgery, that interval can be shortened, sometimes even to zero, works best if you have an expert use ultrasound to check you’re exercising correctly, also works great after childbirth or for anyone experiencing general sphincter entropy.

  15. That relationships—one of the great drivers of happiness—if you want better relationships, you can probably achieve that by deliberately increasing your level of relationship “skill”, which is done by following boring standard relationship best practices.

  16. That due to how spermatogonial stem cells are activated, one testicle produces only gametes with an X chromosome and the other only gametes with a Y chromosome so if you’re going to lose a testicle you might want to freeze some sperm, that sounds plausible, that’s what Anaxagoras thought, but thankfully it is completely false, and also that if you lose a testicle, you lose half of testosterone production, but your brain notices and spits out extra leuteinizing hormone, rallying Leydig cells in the remaining testicle and holding testosterone levels constant, no problem.

  17. That trauma care, if you were gunshot in 1964 and still alive when EMS arrived, your odds of surviving were ~66% while today they are ~90%, as our society, despite its seeming disorder, has methodically stacked EMS, 911, regional trauma centers, surgical innovations, police cruiser transport, better imaging, new drugs, statistical lessons on tourniquets / saline / blood ratios, and now prehospital whole blood transfusions.

  18. That each year, 8.2×10¹⁷ kWh of energy from the sun intersects the surface of Earth, while the average human uses 2.1×10⁴ kWh, which with 8.1×10⁹ humans is 4823 times less, thankfully, so even if you did something stupid like grow a C₄ plant like corn with a full-year capture efficiency of only 0.5%, you could in principle get ‘er done by covering 1/(4823×0.005) ≈ 4.1% of the Earth in glorious corn, which, OK, exceeds the 3% currently used as farmland, but if you use 20% efficient solar panels that drops to 0.1%, the amount we currently use for barley.

  19. That the fraction of power lost to resistance going down a wire is (power) × (resistance) / (voltage)², which goes up when power goes up, which is bad, and to decrease resistance by 10× requires putting 10× more material into your wires, which is also bad, but instead you could increase voltage, but if you send 12,470-volt wires into people’s homes they will die from electrocution or fires, so maybe you should drop the voltage close to their home, good idea, but if it’s the late 1800s, then you’ll find that transforming voltage is hard, but perhaps instead of sending electrons in one direction, you can have them wiggle back and forth, the wiggles propagating in waves, then you can transform voltage by just wrapping a bunch of wires around an iron core, and now 140 years later we have semiconductors that convert between wiggling and non-wiggling electrons, and sometimes we have chains that go from no wiggles (solar panel) to wiggles (voltage transformer) back to no wiggles (high-voltage transmission line) back to wiggles (voltage transformer + local grid) back to no wiggles (your phone charger), which is good, for some reason.

  20. That public libraries, doing fine in a changing world, currently delivered in the US at a total cost of $50/person.

  21. That alcohol is, on net, probably bad, and young people in rich countries have noticed this and are drinking less, and this has created beautiful economies of scale in specialized yeast and vacuum distillation and membrane filters which are making nonalcoholic beer increasingly cheap and good, which is good, and sadly these don’t work well for wine and not at all for spirits, which is bad, but beer tastes better than those things, technology has delivered in the right place.

  22. That hedonic adaptation, typically an adversary in our quest for galactic bliss-maximization, is also in some respects an ally, most notably if you stop eating processing-maxxed combinations of sugar/salt/fat, you will at first feel deprived but will soon find that roasted carrots taste very sweet and thus you can get the health benefits of healthy food while still enjoying food nearly as much as before, although ironically hedonic adaptation will also likely take hold of those health benefits, limiting how much durable bliss they create, but whatever, I’ll take it.

  23. That if you go to almost any park / forest / mountain, almost anywhere in the world, and you hike 5 km away from the road, it will not be crowded.

  24. That our civilization is constructed along a two-dimensional manifold in three-dimensional space, meaning that if a warhead of energy E is detonated, the energy delivered to civilization scales as E²ᐟ³, and if E > 10 megatons, then energy starts to vent out into space, dropping the energy delivered to E¹ᐟ² or even lower, so if you wanted to destroy mainland Spain with a single blastwave (please don’t) you’d need a 30 teraton weapon (2 billion Hiroshimas, 1300 copies of peak early 1960s global arsenal, ⅓ Chicxulub), and to build that you’d either need to mine 400 billion tons of uranium ore (60× known land reserves), or to filter 1 million tons of deuterium out of water (1-2 years of global electricity production) and then store it at -250 °C in a tank 20 times larger than an oil supertanker and covered in millions of tons of lead, or you could make do with only 275 thousand tons of deuterium and drop the -250 °C tank but then you’ll need to mine 12 million tons of lithium (40% of known lithium reserves), seems hard.

  25. That if you’re OK using fire instead of a blastwave, then note that while blastwaves bend along the atmosphere, X-rays and thermal radiation need line of sight, and that to get a decent angle on all of mainland Spain, you’d need to detonate somewhere like 500 km out in space, but then 90% of the X-rays won’t be pointed towards Spain, and X-rays can’t fly through air, so instead your goal is to turn the upper atmosphere above Spain into a superheated plasma that absorbs the X-rays and re-emits light at lower frequencies, but then half of that light goes back out into space and much of the rest is lost to ozone or dust or clouds, and the energy pulse stretches to several seconds, the physics are insanely complicated but the consensus is that you’re better off dropping down to 50 km and hoping the fireball peeks over the horizon, and it happens that the atmosphere is ~90 km high which means a single fireball can just barely see all of mainland Spain, so a 20-40 gigaton weapon (1-2× early 1960s global arsenal) might ignite the flammable parts of Spain on a cloudless day, which is bad, but short of building an artificial asteroid, Earth’s curvature does seem to make it quasi-impossible for a single detonation to destroy anything larger than Spain, thankfully, I guess.

  26. That there’s still interest in watching humans spell and play chess and run fast, hopefully a prelude.

  27. That if you were born before ~1993 (earlier in Japan and South Korea, later in Europe) you were likely infected with VZV and got chickenpox, but before the virus was killed, it injected copies of its DNA into some of your ganglia, mostly near the spine or brainstem, and ganglia don’t die, so that DNA is still there today, floating around with your chromosomes, and rarely your ganglia transcribe it and make new VZV, but your immune system kills it, but as you age, the virus may someday travel down a nerve pathway to your skin, causing lots of pain, which is bad, but that need not happen because the shingles vaccine exists, thankfully, and also that if you were born after ~1993, you likely got the chickenpox vaccine and never got chickenpox but—surprise—you still have VZV DNA in your ganglia because that vaccine contains live virus, but it’s of a weakened strain so your risk of getting shingles is somewhat unclear, maybe you’ll still need the vaccine someday, but if you don’t get it and you do get shingles, it will likely happen in the same part of the body where you were injected with the chickenpox vaccine decades before, which is fun.

  28. That we are very cynical these days, but when someone says, I am doing X because I think Y, and everyone responds, nuh-uh, you are doing X because you think Z, upon close inspection often they really do think Y, and while recognizing this generally doesn’t make it easier to get them to stop doing X, it makes the world look a bit brighter.

  29. That during the peak of the cold war, some people figured that we were doomed and decided it was better not to have children, which even looking back now doesn’t seem like a totally crazy decision, but most people didn’t decide that, thankfully.

  30. That the best way to preserve a car is to keep it in the garage and only drive it slowly to church on Sundays, and you might expect the human animal to work the same way, forcing you choose when to “spend” yourself, but for the most part it seems to be the opposite, the way to keep your mind and body working is to drive them a lot, at high speeds, to new places.

title: Las Vegas, Monte Carlo, and Integer Factorization
content:
Monte Carlo algorithms typically have a fixed runtime but a variable error rate.

Las Vegas algorithms have a variable runtime but a fixed (i.e. zero) error rate.

Stanisław Ulam came up with the idea of Monte Carlo methods in 1946 and Nicholas Metropolis coined the term “Monte Carlo” the next year.

László Babai coined the term “Las Vegas algorithm” in 1979 as a pun on Monte Carlo.

Las Vegas factoring algorithm in the news

There’s a new paper on GitHub titled Unconditional Integer Factorization in Time LN[1/3, O(1)]. It is a Las Vegas algorithm because it always [1] returns a correct factorization, though the time it takes to execute is random.

What is unconditional about the new algorithm? The analysis of the new algorithm does not depend on any unproven assumptions. Before there was a proof of the (Generalized) Riemann Hypothesis, many theorems were conditional because they assumed the GRH. The fastest integer factorization algorithms are not dependent on GRH but are dependent on other widely believed but unproven conjectures.

The notation LN[α, c], commonly used in computational number theory, stands for

exp(c (log N)α (log log N)1−α)

The fastest commonly used factorization method at this time is the GNFS (general number field sieve). Its runtime is

LN[1/3, (64/9)1/3 + o(1)] ≈ LN[1/3, 1.923]

This means that the c term is (64/9)1/3 = 1.923 plus a term that goes to zero as N increases.

For the new algorithm, the α term is the same as GNFS but the c term is something less than 105. This is a bound on the worst-case expected time. The runtime is not as good as GNFS but the runtime proof does not depend on any unproven assumptions. The best unconditional algorithm before this recent result was LN[1/2, 1].

 

[1] Las Vegas algorithms halt with probability 1. In practice they terminate, but strictly speaking they are partial functions, functions that give a correct result when they terminate.

The post Las Vegas, Monte Carlo, and Integer Factorization first appeared on John D. Cook.
